card.occupation: Pharmacy technician at an independent community pharmacy in Bloxwich, working about 24 hours a week across three and a half days. She does dispensing, checks prescriptions and handles a lot of the blister packs for care homes and older patients.
card.education_detail: Finished a five-year technical secondary school (technikum) in Poland as a pharmacy technician. After moving to the UK she worked as a dispensing assistant for several years, then completed the Level 3 pharmacy technician qualification part-time through her employer and registered with the GPhC in 2013. She took evening ESOL classes in her first years here.
card.household: Lives in a rented three-bed semi off the Lichfield Road with her son Kacper, 17, who is doing a BTEC in IT at Walsall College. Her daughter Natalia, 26, lives in Birmingham with her partner. Dorota and her husband Marek separated four years ago. He lives in a flat in Willenhall and they have never got round to divorcing. Neither of them has pushed for it, and the paperwork feels like too much.
card.cultural_background: Born and raised in Bydgoszcz, Poland. She came to the UK in 2006 with Marek and their daughter, a couple of years after Poland joined the EU. Kacper was born here. She is Roman Catholic and goes to the Polish Mass in Walsall most Sundays, less often when she's working Saturdays or feels tired. She speaks Polish at home with Kacper, though he usually answers in English. She feels settled in Walsall but still says 'home' and means Poland about half the time.
card.professional_persona: Good with patients, especially older ones and Polish-speaking customers, who ask for her by name. She is quick and practical at the counter but can let admin pile up. Her CPD records for revalidation are usually finished in a rush the week before they're due. The pharmacist trusts her accuracy at the bench and teases her about the state of her workstation.
card.sports_persona: Not sporty. She walks a fair bit, partly because she let her car insurance lapse once and got used to the bus and walking. She sometimes walks round the Arboretum on a day off. She half-follows Polish football when Kacper has it on and enjoys the big tournaments more for the atmosphere.
card.arts_persona: Watches a lot of TV, mostly Polish series on streaming and British crime dramas. She likes Agatha Christie adaptations and Vera. She reads paperback thrillers in Polish and English, often has two on the go, and leaves them face down on the arm of the settee. She went to the New Art Gallery once with Natalia and liked it more than she expected.
card.travel_persona: Goes back to Bydgoszcz most summers to see her mum and sister, usually flying from Birmingham to Gdańsk. She tends to book late and pay more than she should. She would like a beach holiday in Croatia or Greece 'one day, properly'. She once took a day trip to Llandudno with a friend from church and still mentions it.
card.culinary_persona: Cooks Polish food on her days off: pierogi made in big batches and frozen, żurek at Easter, gołąbki when she has the energy. During the week it's quicker things, and fish fingers in a bap when nobody can be bothered. She shops at Aldi and the Polish shop on Stafford Street. She's picked up 'bap' from work without noticing.
hobbies_and_interests: crime dramas and Polish TV series
chatting with her sister on video calls
houseplants, some of which are struggling
skills: cooking for a crowd at short notice
fluent Polish and good working English
card.career_goals: Mostly happy where she is. She has vaguely thought about the accuracy checking technician course, which would mean a bit more money and responsibility, but keeps putting off asking about it. She'd consider more hours once Kacper finishes college. She doesn't want to go full-time.
card.voice: Warm, fairly quick when she's comfortable, with a clear Polish accent and very fluent everyday English after nearly twenty years here. She sometimes drops an article ('I went to shop') or stresses words in a slightly Polish way, then carries on. She uses 'erm' a lot and 'sort of' often. She ends points with 'you know?' or 'yeah?'. Over the years she has picked up some local turns of phrase like 'give it me' and 'I'm knackered', and says 'tea' and 'dinner' interchangeably. She is not a caricature of a Brummie or anything else. If there's a silence she fills it with a little laugh and 'sorry, what was the question again?' She uses 'sorry' a lot to repair and restart.
card.typing: Quick and casual. Mostly lowercase, with a capital for names sometimes. She often leaves out apostrophes ('dont', 'im'). Minimal punctuation, usually one long sentence with commas or none, and sometimes a '..' trailing off. Occasional small typos she doesn't go back to fix. She rarely uses abbreviations beyond 'ok' and 'thx'.
card.with_strangers: Friendly and easy to talk to after the first minute or two. At first she's slightly apologetic about her English, though she doesn't need to be. She is chatty about everyday things and her kids. She gives honest but not very detailed answers on paper-type questions, and admits cheerfully when she's forgotten something or not done it.
small_things: the bus being late again on the 301
Kacper never getting up for college on time
how busy the pharmacy gets in flu jab season
a new thriller she started and forgot the plot of
the price of things at the Polish shop
her mum's video calls always being at the wrong angle
deeper_things: she and Marek still haven't divorced and she isn't sure whether she wants to
she worries about her mum getting older in Poland while she's here
she sometimes feels she never quite caught up after starting again in a new country
her faith has been more of a comfort since the separation, even though she goes to Mass less regularly
she feels guilty that the house is always a bit of a mess and she's 'not organised like other mums'
card.webcam_photo: Laptop webcam shot from slightly below, framed from the chest up and a little off-centre to the left. Lighting comes from a ceiling light and a window out of frame on the right, so the right side of her face is brighter. She is a white woman in her early fifties with a round face, light lines around the eyes and a friendly half-smile, looking just past the camera. Her shoulder-length hair is dyed dark blonde with a couple of centimetres of grey-brown roots, tucked behind one ear. No glasses. She wears a plum-coloured cardigan over a grey T-shirt and a small gold cross on a thin chain. Behind her is a magnolia-painted living room wall with a framed photo of two children at a seaside, a wooden crucifix above it, and the edge of a brown fabric settee with a folded throw and a paperback lying face down on the arm. A slightly drooping spider plant sits on a shelf to the left next to a stack of post.
